---
title: "Code Regression"
---

The code-regression setup asks whether we can predict execution-memory
statistics from source code. Our current slice takes the CDSS rows from the
[Code-Regression dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/akhauriyash/Code-Regression)
and predicts the memory target from the submitted program text. The broader
dataset and RegressLM baseline are described in
[Regression Language Models for Code](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26476); our
current model family uses [T5Gemma](https://huggingface.co/google/t5gemma-s-s-prefixlm)
encoders and compares supervised regression with rollout-based MaxRL methods
from [Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02710).

### Overview

::: {.callout-note title="Main thread"}
This writeup studies scalar CDSS memory prediction from source code. We track
two target variants: raw `memory_bytes` and a per-language quantile-normalized
memory score. The experiments then branch into three training routes. CE
pretraining follows a RegressLM-style text-to-number recipe and learns one
canonical P10 tokenization of the label. LM-RLOO and LM-MaxRL keep the
language-model decoder while using sampled token sequences as latent rollouts:
each rollout is parsed back to a number and scored against the scalar label. The
regression-head route predicts one scalar directly and trains it with SL-MSE,
RLOO, or MaxRL. The organizing distinction is between objectives over a token
representation and objectives over scalar prediction error.
:::

## Problem setup

Each row is a code submission with metadata and a scalar memory target. After
preprocessing, we keep only CDSS examples and format the model input as

```text
# CDSS
# Language: Python
<source code>
```

where `Python` is replaced by the metadata language when available. The
prediction target has two current forms:

- **Raw memory**. `target = memory_bytes`, copied from the original dataset
  target column after filtering finite CDSS rows.
- **Per-language quantile-normalized memory**. Within each CDSS language, raw
  memory values are ranked and mapped through the standard normal inverse CDF.
  This keeps ordering inside each language while removing language-specific
  scale and marginal-shape differences.

Let $X$ denote the formatted code prompt, $Y_{\mathrm{raw}}$ the raw memory
value, and $Y_{\mathrm{qn}}$ the quantile-normalized value. In either variant
the supervised target is a scalar
$$
Y \in \mathbb{R},
$$
and the ideal predictor is the conditional mean
$$
g^\ast(x) := \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X=x].
$$
The main held-out risk is therefore
$$
\mathcal{E}(\theta)
  :=
  \mathbb{E}\left[(g_\theta(X)-Y)^2\right].
$$

The raw target is the literal memory-prediction task. The quantile-normalized
target turns the question toward within-language ranking and calibration: can
the model place a submission correctly relative to other submissions in the same
programming language? Performance on this normalized target should be read as
evidence about relative memory behavior inside each language. Raw-byte
performance additionally tests whether the model can handle the cross-language
unit scale.

Output-side tokenization adds one more layer of notation. Let
$$
\mathcal{Z}
$$
be the finite set of syntactically valid decoder token sequences under the P10
grammar, and let
$$
\phi:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}
$$
be the deterministic parser that extracts the numeric value represented by a
complete token sequence. A language-model decoder defines a conditional
distribution
$$
q_\theta(z\mid x),\qquad z\in\mathcal{Z}.
$$
The latent rollout is the token sequence $Z\sim q_\theta(\cdot\mid x)$; the
decoded prediction candidate is the scalar $\phi(Z)$.

The targeted regression problem follows the scalar label $Y$. Token strings
enter as one way to produce candidate numeric values. For example, if the final
predictor is the median of decoded samples, then the induced predictor is
$$
m_\theta(x) := \operatorname{median}\{\phi(Z):Z\sim q_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\},
$$
and the corresponding scalar risk is
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[(m_\theta(X)-Y)^2\right].
$$
Training methods below use different surrogates for this target. Many token
sequences can parse to the same number:
$$
\mathcal{Z}(v) := \{z\in\mathcal{Z}: \phi(z)=v\}
$$
can contain several valid strings.

## Canonical recipe

| Knob | Current value |
|---|---|
| Data source | CDSS subset of `akhauriyash/Code-Regression` |
| Input | `# CDSS`, language header, then submitted source code |
| Targets | raw `memory_bytes` and per-language quantile-normalized memory |
| Encoder | `google/t5gemma-s-s-prefixlm` through the local T5Gemma wrapper |
| Default encoder training | frozen unless `--train-encoder` is passed |
| Max input length | 2048 encoder tokens |
| Optimizer | Adafactor |
| Default learning rate | `5e-3` |
| LR schedule | 10% warmup, then cosine decay to zero |
| Precision | bfloat16 autocast on CUDA |
| Gradient clipping | max norm `2.0` |
| Modal pretraining default | 2000 steps, total batch 2048, device batch 64, 8 GPUs |
| CE eval aggregation | sample 64 numeric decodes per example, then take the median |
| Modal LM-RLOO / LM-MaxRL default | 2000 steps, total batch 2048, device batch 32, 8 token rollouts, rollout temperature `1.0` |
| LM-MaxRL score std | `1.0` |
| Modal regression-head default | 2000 steps, total batch 2048, device batch 256 |
| Evaluation cap | 256 examples per retained CDSS language in the Modal recipes |
| Regression-head RLOO / MaxRL rollout default | 128 Gaussian rollouts, rollout std `1.0` |

## Methods

The current methods combine two related architectures with three objective
families. CE pretraining and LM-RL both use an encoder-decoder language model
over numeric target tokens. CE learns the canonical token string itself.
LM-RLOO and LM-MaxRL sample token strings, parse them to numbers, and optimize
scalar reward or likelihood of the parsed value. The regression-head route keeps
the T5Gemma encoder idea and predicts through a direct scalar value head, trained
with SL-MSE, RLOO, or MaxRL.

### CE pretraining - text-to-number language modeling

`pretrain_code_regression` trains a RegressLM-style conditional decoder. The
encoder reads the code prompt, and the decoder autoregressively emits a fixed
P10 scientific-notation representation of the scalar target. With the default
P10 tokenizer, one number uses

$$
2 + d = 6
$$

tokens: one sign token, four mantissa digit tokens, and one exponent token. For
example, under the default four-digit P10 representation,

```text
256.0   -> <+> <2> <5> <6> <0> <E-1>
-1.25   -> <-> <1> <2> <5> <0> <E-3>
0.1234  -> <+> <1> <2> <3> <4> <E-4>
```

The table below shows representative raw and quantile-normalized CDSS targets
under this P10 tokenization.

```{=html}
<div class="scaled-plotly-frame" data-source-width="1000" data-source-height="1350">
  <iframe src="assets/code-regression/cdss-target-tokenization-samples.html"
          title="CDSS target tokenization samples"
          scrolling="no"
          onload="window.fitScaledIframeContainer(this.parentElement);"></iframe>
</div>
```

The important detail is that training is ordinary language modeling. If
$c(Y) = (Z^c_1,\dots,Z^c_L)$ is the canonical target tokenization of the
numeric label, the model minimizes token-level cross entropy
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\theta)
  =
  -\mathbb{E}
  \left[
    \frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}
      \log q_\theta(Z^c_\ell \mid X, Z^c_{<\ell})
  \right].
$$

::: {.callout-note title="CE learns a numeric spelling"}
CE pretraining learns a symbolic sign-digit-exponent sequence. Numeric scale
enters through the tokenizer's rounding, clipping, and exponent range, so a
single token error can have very different scalar consequences depending on
whether it lands in the mantissa or exponent. The digit targets are discrete
classes: predicting `<6>` means assigning probability to the token class `<6>`.
This makes CE a useful RegressLM-style baseline and also makes token likelihood
an indirect proxy for numeric MSE.
:::

There is an additional representation issue. The P10 grammar allows valid
non-canonical strings with leading zero mantissas, and multiple valid strings
can decode to exactly the same number. For example,

```text
<+> <1> <0> <0> <0> <E-3>  -> 1.0
<+> <0> <1> <0> <0> <E-2>  -> 1.0
<+> <0> <0> <1> <0> <E-1>  -> 1.0
<+> <0> <0> <0> <1> <E0>   -> 1.0
```

CE assigns training mass to the single string selected by the canonicalizer
$c(y)$. Numerically equivalent strings receive no target mass under this CE
objective, even though $\phi(z)$ is correct. When the exact label falls outside
the finite P10 grid or between grid points, the canonicalizer first rounds or
clips to a representable token string. Thus the CE
population target is
$$
q^\ast_{\mathrm{CE}}(z\mid x)
  =
  \mathbb{P}(c(Y)=z\mid X=x),
$$
The corresponding set-valued numeric target is
$$
\mathcal{Z}(Y)=\{z:\phi(z)=Y\}.
$$
For deterministic labels and infinite model capacity this distinction can be
small, because the canonical string decodes to a good numeric approximation. For
finite models it matters: probability mass on a numerically equivalent
non-canonical rollout helps scalar prediction while receiving no CE credit.

Decoding is also language-model-like. At each decoder step, impossible P10
tokens are masked out: the first position can only be a sign, middle positions
are digits, and the final position is an exponent token. Evaluation samples 64
complete numeric decodes per example and reports the median decoded value before
computing scalar metrics.

### LM-RL - token rollouts with scalar rewards

LM-RL keeps the same constrained language-model policy as CE and changes the
object being optimized. We draw rollout token sequences from the model itself:
$$
Z_j \sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid x),\qquad j=1,\dots,R,
$$
where $T>0$ is the sampling temperature used for both sampling and sequence
log-probabilities. Each rollout is parsed to a scalar
$$
V_j := \phi(Z_j).
$$
The loss functions then compare $V_j$ to the exact target value $y$ stored in
the dataset. The learning signal rewards token strings whose extracted number is
close to $y$.

The sequence score used by policy gradients is
$$
\log q_{\theta,T}(Z_j\mid x)
  =
  \sum_{\ell=1}^L
  \log q_{\theta,T}(Z_{j,\ell}\mid x,Z_{j,<\ell}),
$$
with the same P10 validity mask as CE decoding. The sampled scalar values are
detached when constructing rewards or score weights; gradients flow through the
sequence log-probability.

#### LM-RLOO

LM-RLOO uses negative squared scalar error as the reward:
$$
r_j := -(V_j-y)^2.
$$
For $R\geq 2$ rollouts, the leave-one-out advantage is
$$
A_j
  =
  r_j - \frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{k\ne j} r_k
  =
  \frac{R}{R-1}(r_j-\bar r),
\qquad
\bar r := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k=1}^R r_k.
$$
The minibatch surrogate minimized in code is
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{LM\mbox{-}RLOO}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{BR}
  \sum_{b=1}^B\sum_{j=1}^R
    A_{b,j}\log q_{\theta,T}(Z_{b,j}\mid x_b),
$$
where $A_{b,j}$ is detached. The corresponding population objective is
$$
J_{\mathrm{LM\mbox{-}RLOO}}(\theta)
  =
  \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}
  \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid X)}
  \left[-(\phi(Z)-Y)^2\right].
$$
Equivalently, LM-RLOO minimizes the expected squared error of decoded token
rollouts:
$$
\mathbb{E}_{X,Y,Z}\left[(\phi(Z)-Y)^2\right].
$$
Thus all token strings with the same decoded value are interchangeable to
LM-RLOO. If $\phi(z)=y$ exactly, the reward is zero regardless of whether $z$ is
the canonical P10 string.

#### LM-MaxRL

LM-MaxRL replaces the raw squared-error reward by a normalized Gaussian
likelihood score. Let $\tau>0$ denote `score_std`. For a rollout $z$, define
$$
s_\tau(y,z)
  :=
  \exp\left(-\frac{(\phi(z)-y)^2}{2\tau^2}\right)
  \in (0,1].
$$
This is the Gaussian observation likelihood
$\mathcal{N}(y;\phi(z),\tau^2)$ divided by its supremum
$(\sqrt{2\pi}\tau)^{-1}$, so the maximum possible score is one. For one example,
the marginal normalized likelihood under the LM policy is
$$
S_{\theta,\tau}(x,y)
  :=
  \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid x)}
  [s_\tau(y,Z)].
$$

The degree-$D$ MaxRL target is the truncated log-likelihood objective
$$
J_D(\theta)
  =
  \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}
  \left[
    -\sum_{k=1}^{D}
    \frac{(1-S_{\theta,\tau}(X,Y))^k}{k}
  \right].
$$
As $D\to\infty$ this becomes
$$
J_\infty(\theta)
  =
  \mathbb{E}_{X,Y}\left[\log S_{\theta,\tau}(X,Y)\right].
$$

The sampled implementation uses the same leave-one-out MaxRL estimator described
in [MaxRL gradient estimator details](gradient-estimator.qmd). For sampled
scores $s_j=s_\tau(y,Z_j)$, define complements $a_j=1-s_j$. The leave-one-out
weight for rollout $j$ is
$$
\omega_j
  =
  \sum_{k=0}^{D-1}
  \frac{e_k((a_i)_{i\ne j})}{\binom{R-1}{k}},
$$
where $e_k$ is the $k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial and $e_0=1$. The
current LM-MaxRL recipe always subtracts a rollout baseline:
$$
s^{\mathrm{eff}}_j
  =
  \frac{R}{R-1}(s_j-\bar s),
\qquad
\bar s := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{i=1}^{R}s_i.
$$
The surrogate loss is
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{LM\mbox{-}MaxRL}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{BR}
  \sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
    \omega_{b,j}s^{\mathrm{eff}}_{b,j}
    \log q_{\theta,T}(Z_{b,j}\mid x_b),
$$
with the weights detached. By default, the implementation uses $D=R$ unless a
separate degree is provided.

#### Optimization targets and limits

The CE and LM-RL methods can share a decoder and tokenizer while optimizing
different population quantities:

| Method | Population target | What is treated as correct? |
|---|---|---|
| CE pretraining | Maximize $\mathbb{E}[\log q_\theta(c(Y)\mid X)]$ token by token | Only the canonical token string $c(Y)$ |
| LM-RLOO | Maximize $\mathbb{E}[-(\phi(Z)-Y)^2]$ for $Z\sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid X)$ | Any rollout whose decoded number is close to $Y$ |
| LM-MaxRL | Maximize $J_D$ or, as $D\to\infty$, $\mathbb{E}[\log \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim q_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid X)}s_\tau(Y,Z)]$ | Any rollout with high Gaussian score after decoding |

::: {.callout-note title="Shared decoder, different target"}
CE, LM-RLOO, and LM-MaxRL can use the same P10 decoder while learning from
different signals. CE concentrates probability on a canonical string. LM-RLOO
and LM-MaxRL score decoded scalar values, so token strings that parse to the
same useful number are equivalent for the rollout objective.
:::

CE has no training rollout count or score standard deviation. As the evaluation
sample count grows, its reported median prediction converges to the median of
$\phi(Z)$ under the learned decoder distribution. This affects evaluation Monte
Carlo error while leaving the CE training target unchanged.

As the number of LM-RL training rollouts $R$ grows, LM-RLOO converges to the
exact policy gradient of $J_{\mathrm{LM\mbox{-}RLOO}}$. The leave-one-out
baseline leaves the population target unchanged and changes estimator variance.
LM-MaxRL converges to the gradient of the degree-$D$ MaxRL target when $D$ is
fixed. Under the default choice $D=R$, sending $R\to\infty$ also sends
$D\to\infty$, so the target approaches the log marginal score $J_\infty$.

The `score_std` limit only applies directly to LM-MaxRL and is separate from
the rollout sampling temperature. LM-RLOO has no `score_std` hyperparameter in
the current implementation. For LM-MaxRL:

- As $\tau\to 0$, $s_\tau(y,z)$ approaches an indicator of exact numeric
  equality $\phi(z)=y$. If $y$ is exactly representable, the limiting objective
  rewards the total probability of all exact representations
  $\sum_{z:\phi(z)=y}q_\theta(z\mid x)$, including non-canonical strings. If
  $y$ falls between representable decoded values, the signal concentrates on the
  nearest grid points and can become extremely sparse in finite rollouts.
- As $\tau\to\infty$,
  $s_\tau(y,z)=1-(\phi(z)-y)^2/(2\tau^2)+O(\tau^{-4})$. Therefore
  $\log S_{\theta,\tau}(x,y)$ is
  $-\mathbb{E}_{Z}[(\phi(Z)-y)^2]/(2\tau^2)+O(\tau^{-4})$ up to constants. The
  target becomes expected decoded MSE, and the gradient scale vanishes like
  $\tau^{-2}$.

For LM-RLOO, introducing an artificial reward scale
$-(\phi(z)-y)^2/(2\tau^2)$ would leave the optimum unchanged for any finite
$\tau>0$ and would simply rescale the gradient. The current code fixes this
scale implicitly by using $-(\phi(z)-y)^2$.

### Regression-head model

The regression-head methods use a deterministic scalar predictor
$$
g_\theta(x) \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
The architecture is a T5Gemma encoder, a learned one-token query passed through
a transformer decoder over the encoder memory, and a linear value head. In
code, the model predicts from the decoded query state:
$$
g_\theta(x)
  =
  w^\top h_\theta(x) + b.
$$

This architecture removes the numeric tokenizer from the output side. The model
is judged directly in the same scalar space as the target variant being trained:
raw bytes for the raw task, or normal scores for the quantile-normalized task.

### SL-MSE - direct scalar regression

The supervised regression baseline minimizes the same squared error used by the
primary evaluation:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SL\mbox{-}MSE}}(\theta)
  =
  \mathbb{E}\left[(g_\theta(X)-Y)^2\right].
$$

For a minibatch,
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{SL\mbox{-}MSE}}
  =
  \frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}
    (g_\theta(x_b)-y_b)^2.
$$

This is the cleanest reference objective: if the evaluation target is MSE, then
SL-MSE optimizes it directly. It uses no rollouts, likelihood temperatures,
tokenization choices, or policy-gradient estimator.

### RLOO - Gaussian rollout policy with leave-one-out rewards

RLOO turns the scalar predictor into the mean of a Gaussian rollout policy:
$$
Z_j \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid x)
      =
      \mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x), \sigma^2),
\qquad j=1,\dots,R.
$$

The reward is negative squared error against the scalar target:
$$
r_j = -(Z_j - y)^2.
$$

The leave-one-out advantage is
$$
A_j
  =
  r_j - \frac{1}{R-1}\sum_{k\ne j}r_k
  =
  \frac{R}{R-1}(r_j-\bar r),
\qquad
\bar r := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{k=1}^{R}r_k.
$$

The score-function surrogate is
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{RLOO}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{BR}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
    A_{b,j}\,
    \log \pi_\theta(Z_{b,j}\mid x_b),
$$
with the sampled advantages detached.

The leave-one-out baseline is unbiased because it depends only on peer rollouts
for the current example. In the population limit,
$$
\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x),\sigma^2)}
  [-(Z-y)^2]
  =
  -(g_\theta(x)-y)^2 - \sigma^2.
$$
The extra $\sigma^2$ term is independent of $\theta$, so maximizing expected
RLOO reward has the same optimum and gradient direction as minimizing scalar
MSE. Finite $R$ changes the variance of the gradient estimator while preserving
the population target.

### MaxRL - likelihood-weighted rollout estimator

MaxRL uses the same Gaussian rollout policy,
$$
Z_j \sim \mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x),\sigma^2),
$$
and scores each rollout by a Gaussian observation likelihood of the target:
$$
\ell_y(z)
  =
  \mathcal{N}(y; z, \sigma^2).
$$

The supremum of this one-dimensional likelihood is
$$
L = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma},
$$
so the normalized likelihood is
$$
\sigma_j
  :=
  \frac{\ell_y(Z_j)}{L}
  =
  \exp\left(-\frac{(Z_j-y)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)
  \in (0,1].
$$

For one example, define the marginal normalized likelihood
$$
\sigma_\theta(x,y)
  :=
  \mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}
    [\sigma_y(Z)].
$$
The degree-$M$ MaxRL objective is the same truncation used in
[MaxRL gradient estimator details](gradient-estimator.qmd):
$$
J_M(\theta)
  =
  -\sum_{k=1}^{M}
    \frac{(1-\sigma_\theta)^k}{k}.
$$
As $M\to\infty$, this approaches
$$
J_\infty(\theta) = \log \sigma_\theta.
$$

The sampled estimator forms leave-one-out weights from the peer complements
$a_i = 1-\sigma_i$. For rollout $j$,
$$
\omega_j
  =
  \sum_{k=0}^{M-1}
  \frac{
    e_k((a_i)_{i\ne j})
  }{
    \binom{R-1}{k}
  },
$$
where $e_k$ is the $k$-th elementary symmetric polynomial. With baseline
subtraction, the effective normalized likelihood term is
$$
\sigma^{\mathrm{eff}}_j
  =
  \frac{R}{R-1}(\sigma_j-\bar\sigma),
\qquad
\bar\sigma := \frac{1}{R}\sum_{i=1}^{R}\sigma_i.
$$
The policy-gradient surrogate is
$$
\widehat{\mathcal{L}}_{\mathrm{MaxRL}}
  =
  -\frac{1}{BR}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{j=1}^{R}
    \omega_{b,j}\sigma^{\mathrm{eff}}_{b,j}
    \log \pi_\theta(Z_{b,j}\mid x_b),
$$
with the score weights detached.

In the exact Gaussian limit, MaxRL also reduces to MSE. The convolution identity
gives
$$
\mathbb{E}_{Z\sim\mathcal{N}(g_\theta(x),\sigma^2)}
  [\mathcal{N}(y;Z,\sigma^2)]
  =
  \mathcal{N}(y;g_\theta(x),2\sigma^2),
$$
so
$$
\log \sigma_\theta(x,y)
  =
  -\frac{(g_\theta(x)-y)^2}{4\sigma^2}
  + \mathrm{const}.
$$
Thus the infinite-rollout MaxRL objective is a positive rescaling of negative
MSE plus a constant. As with RLOO, the finite-rollout estimator is the
interesting object: it changes how noisy or selective the update is while the
ideal scalar target remains MSE in this Gaussian setup.

## Evaluation

This writeup focuses on CDSS metrics. The primary keys are

| Metric key | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `eval-core/mse/space/CDSS` | pooled CDSS mean squared error |
| `eval-core/mae/space/CDSS` | pooled CDSS mean absolute error |
| `eval-core/spearman/space/CDSS` | pooled CDSS Spearman rank correlation |

```{=html}
<div class="scaled-plotly-frame" data-source-width="1000" data-source-height="2200">
  <iframe src="assets/code-regression/evaluation-by-language.html"
          title="Step-2000 Spearman by CDSS language"
          scrolling="no"
          onload="window.fitScaledIframeContainer(this.parentElement);"></iframe>
</div>
```

### Evaluation set construction

The eval set is balanced by CDSS language. For each `cdss_language/<language>`
group, the cache builder keeps at most `eval_cap_per_group` examples; in the
current Modal recipes this cap is 256. Languages with at least 256 valid CDSS
examples enter the evaluation. Thus, if $|\mathcal{L}|$ languages survive the
threshold, the pooled CDSS eval set contains exactly
$$
256 \cdot |\mathcal{L}|
$$
examples, with the same number of examples from each retained language.

Selection is deterministic: examples are ordered by a stable hash of their
identifier, then capped within language. Each retained row is assigned both its
auxiliary language group, such as `cdss_language/Python`, and the pooled
`space/CDSS` group.

The pooled CDSS metric treats all selected CDSS eval examples as one population.
For MSE, with selected CDSS pairs $(y_i,\hat y_i)$,
$$
\widehat{\mathrm{MSE}}_{\mathrm{CDSS}}
  =
  \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(\hat y_i-y_i)^2.
$$
MAE is the same pooled average with absolute error, and Spearman is computed
once over the pooled CDSS target and prediction vectors.

Language-mean metrics shift the estimand. The auxiliary
`cdss_language/<language>` groups first compute a metric within each language.
Then `eval-core/<metric>/space/CDSS_language_mean` averages those language
scores equally:
$$
\widehat{m}_{\mathrm{language\ mean}}
  =
  \frac{1}{|\mathcal{L}|}
  \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal{L}}
    \widehat{m}_\ell.
$$

The decoder-LM and regression-head routes produce predictions differently
before metrics are computed:

- CE pretraining, LM-RLOO, and LM-MaxRL sample numeric decodes and use the
  per-example median decoded value as the prediction.
- Regression-head methods produce one deterministic scalar prediction
  $g_\theta(x)$.

After that, all methods are evaluated with the same target/prediction metric
code.
